review_text:
This was just delicious! I just made this for dinner this evening and everyone in the house just ate it up! The sauce is just the best thing about this recipe.
I made this recipe with about 2.5 pounds of chicken and tripled the sauce recipe and just had about enough. I think I would probably make even more sauce next time. I love that the sauce is sweet enough and not overly sour either. It is very tasty and has the right amount of tangy-ness.
I used half of the sugar (and actually used granulated sugar instead of brown) that was called for the recipe (and also to taste) and minced in more garlic than the recipe called for. I also used orange juice and ground ginger instead (was too lazy to cut ginger). I omit the water and used lower sodium soy sauce. I also used sarrachi sauce (to taste) instead of the red pepper flake and used extra ketchup than the recipe calls for because my family likes the sweetness of ketchup in general.
I cooked the chicken w/ a little bit of salt and minced garlic. And since I had so much chicken, I cooked it in batches. After I put the chicken aside and let the sauce simmer for a while, I added in some vegetables (they were frozen and I cooked them separately beforehand and let them drain so that they would not add extra water to the sauce) and the chicken. I didn't cook the chicken all the way to prevent drying out the chicken (I used chicken breast meat). And then just finished the chicken in the pot w/ the sauce. The chicken was moist and juicy.
I will definitely make this again.

review_text: This recipe is excellent. My seasoning adjustments make it taste more like Panera's. My cooking recommendations are what works best for me for a busy weeknight meal. In a pot, add chicken broth. My favorite chicken stock is Better Bouillon paste (keep refrigerated). I add an extra half a cup of liquid bc I will be boiling veggies with lid on. Add the broccoli and carrots. I use frozen chopped broccoli florets with half of the stems removed and a bag of pre-julienned carrots (found in produce section near baby carrots). Boil covered over medium heat for 10 minutes. (This cooking time varies greatly by what kind/size pan you are using and your heat level. Take the lid of often to check. Only boil until carrots are tender.) I use my immersion blender to puree veggie/broth mixture bc my young children will only it eat it pureed. Otherwise, Panera broccoli cheese is NOT pureed. In a separate pan, make white sauce. Over medium heat, Sauté onion in butter. When onions translucent add garlic. Sauté. Turn heat to low. Add flour. Whisk. Slowly add heavy cream (not half and half). Turn heat off. Add cheese. It actually taste more like Panera if you use three cheese powder, but using 1/2 shredded Cabot cheddar cheese and 1/2 American cheese like Velveeta is desirable. This will be very thick. You want it to be! Turn heat back on low white sauce. Slowly add chicken broth broccoli and carrots mixture while whisking into white sauce. Stir in seasoning to your liking 1 tsp. salt, 1/2 tsp. pepper, 1 tsp. paprika, 1 tsp. white wine, 1 tsp. dijon mustard, and 1/2 tsp. hot sauce. (My young children prefer no white wine, 1 tsp dry mustard powder, and 1/4 tsp. hot sauce.) Another note: I have thickened soup with potato starch for gluten free. you can use lactose free real sharp cheddar cheese and soy heavy cream for lactose free options. I normally make Rhodes frozen dinner rolls to accompany this soup. I use the quick method. I defrost frozen rolls in microwave, so they will raise in 1 hour on my hot stove near where I'm cooking. We have green salad and fresh fruit for dessert. Viola.

review_text: I make pizza often. From finding the best dough recipe to the best kind of mozzarella and of course, the best sauce recipe, it’s a never ending journey. Recently I came up with my favorite dough recipe. It’s simple and it reminds me of pizza huts regular crust, not thin. So now I was back to finding a sauce recipe that would do justice to my fantastic dough. I’ve tried all sorts of sauces. Cooked, uncooked. Whole tomatoes, crushed, raw, paste only sauces. I would be satisfied for awhile with some of them but eventually I went back to the drawing board. I like to have things organized in my life. Especially food recipes that I can always count on to be the same quality every time I make them. I came across this recipe for pizza sauce and like all the others, it claimed to be the best. Taste is a matter of opinion and everyone has their own, including myself, but I am the guy who does most of the cooking so unless I love what it tastes like, I won’t make it a second time. My wife is very easy to please when it comes to food. She doesn’t exactly love to cook, but I do. So, like my pizza dough, I needed to find a sauce recipe I could stay with forever. I’m happy to say I will consider this sauce recipe exactly that. Especially considering that I never purchased fennel seed before and when I bought it, at $5 for a container, I was hoping I won’t be stuck with an ingredient I will never be able to use again. Fennel tastes like whats in sausage. I have seen it in sausage but never questioned what that was lol. It makes perfect sense to me that it is a natural ingredient in pizza sauce. Ok, I agree with the opinion that when a recipe is posted, either you follow it to a tee, or don’t tell us how you “improved” it. So I feel when I tell you that all I did was use more than one garlic clove, it’s not like I changed anything about this recipe. A garlic clove can be many sizes right? There are very small ones and medium size and huge ones. I used several small size ones because it’s only going to taste better with more garlic! I read most of the comments. The majority of them gave high ratings and I always go by the comments and suggestions and ratings of most items I purchase now a days. The one particular comment by several people was the thickness concern. Some of you said you added more sauce. I think that’s fine if you add more sauce to thin this out just a little bit because the intended taste will still be there. Too much sauce and the original flavor will be diluted. Anyway, I love this pizza sauce and I will recommend it whenever possible to my friends. Thank you for sharing it!

review_text:
I made these to accompany Christmas dinner last night. They were excellent, but I didn't roast them long enough as they weren't crispy on the outside, like everyone else said. Since the turkey was out of the oven and I had to heat everything (mashed potatoes, turnip puff, nifty carrots) up at the same time in the oven, they probably would have taken longer than 40 minutes. Everythign but the sprouts were ready, so I took them out. Even though they weren't brown and crispy on the outside, they were definitely very tasty! I also used frozen sprouts that I thawed beforehand and they worked out perfectly! I'll definitely make them again when I don't have such a HUGE meal to prepare and I have the time to cook them for the prescribed period of time. I even threw some of the leftovers into Rescued Turkey Stock (#24576) and they worked really well. I wouldn't recco making them on such a huge meal as thxgiving or Christmas unless you are lucky enough to have a convection or two ovens. The time frame with heating everything else up just didn't jive, which was my fault. They still turned out great!
Edited to add:  I made these the other night to serve with Ribeye steak.  This time, I halved the olive oil and added a few splashes of Sesame oil and then tossed the sprouts in that.  They were absolutely fantastic.  I also roasted them in a cooking stone and they roasted alot better and more evenly than when I used a corningware the last time.

review_text: With regard to the following comment:<br/><br/>"I've said it once and I'll say it again there is nothing Irish about Corned Beef and Cabbage..."<br/><br/>This is incorrect. Both corned beef and cabbage are some of the most traditional ingredients in Irish cooking for hundreds of years. There are several texts and entries in historical documents that confirm this - if you had done an internet search it wouldn't have only taken you a few minutes to see this. I see that your profile says you are from Michigan not Ireland - I will give you the benefit of the doubt as you may be from Ireland originally but I am from Ireland and have lived here all my life so I know what I am talking about. If you are from Ireland and your family didn't eat corned beef and cabbage then you are one of the few. <br/><br/>I should also add that this recipe isn't "traditional" for a few reasons but in particular because olive oil is a relatively recent addition to most Irish kitchens nor does red wine feature in "traditional" Irish cooking. I point this out to show you that people in glass houses shouldn't throw stones. <br/><br/>* A note for people who identify themselves as "Irish Americans". I appreciate the desire to identify with your ancestry but you will find actual Irish people do not consider someone as being Irish if their great great grandfather's dog was Irish [Irish humour]. If you are born in America or any other country and have spent all your life there then you are from that county and not Irish. You are only Irish if you were born in Ireland or if you spent the majority of your life, in particular your childhood, in Ireland. I don't say this to be mean or hurtful but because it is something that is extremely irritating to Irish people and it's about time someone told you.

review_text: The most amazing pecan pie EVER! I made this about a month before Thanksgiving, and on Thanksgiving we had a store bought pecan pie that dulled in comparison. Normally I take a big slice, and this time I could only have two bites of the store bought pie!! After making this recipe, I will never be able to look at any other pecan pie, homemade or store bought, the same! It is so so simple to make, and absolutely delicious. I made this for my boyfriend and his roommates and it was gone in a day, and I've been getting requests to make it ever since! <br/><br/>I followed the steps exactly, but I added the butter to the sugar/corn syrup mix after removing it off the heat so it could melt easier. Then I followed the rest of the steps exactly. At first I only baked it for 30 minutes because it looked ready and the pie crust was starting to brown and I didn't want it to burn. I took it out and realized about an hour later that it definitely needed more time in the oven. I was hesitant about putting it back in the oven after it had sat out for so long, but put it back anyway. After an additional 20-25 minutes in the oven, it turned out perfectly! I definitely recommend leaving it the oven for the recommended time, and next time I will reduce the temperature of my boyfriend's oven because I think it is not completely accurate. Not sure if using a glass pie pan had an affect on the quick browning of the pie crust or not, or if the rack being set one higher than the center position of the oven had to do with it. Regardless, this recipe is amazing and DEFINITELY recommended!

review_text: I had to read a lot of review's before giving it a go (as well as Monica's Bakery website). I managed to make it in a respectable state. I coloured the icing baby blue like a poster here did as it was a pic of the slice that appeared in my e-mail. I had not realised until reading that it was not a sponge, but the description didn't fully explain what it was to be & I was confused by 'whole egg'., I've not started to bake cakes until fairly recently. It was denser than sponge, was more like Pound cake & yes, I can see similarities in texture to cornbread in British supermarkets & some I made myself from recipes here/elsewhere. It doesn't taste like cornbread though, it's very sweet & would be even without the icing. One could cut the sugar but it would affect texture but for me, it's a good thing, as it means I won't eat too much of it!! I thought the cake pic looked familiar, my son-in-law made this for my birthday (but with lavender icing & even though his texture seemed different, more moist, the denseness rang a bell - he got it here lol). He's baking me another, my daughter (his wife) is baking a pink one & I've made a blue one & an angel food cake from here. I think I'll have to look for Post-Easter Diet recipes next week!! (I didn't know they were baking too until I rang saying I'd found his recipe). I believe my cake is dryer because my cooker was new at Christmas & it is still giving off fierce heat.

review_text:
I made these with diced Smoked Ham and Aged Garlic White Cheddar. I cut the salt in half because the ham was salty. The eggs were giant and fluffy, which was delightful, and tasted great, though the ham made them slightly watery. You cannot taste the baking powder at all. DH loved them and suggested we try them several ways, perhaps with sausage or with fried country potatoes & parsley flakes stirred in like my Mom makes.

For those having trouble, I think the key here is that you MUST whisk the eggs quite a lot to get air into them (I like to zap them in a blender or food processor for 30 seconds if I'm making a larger batch), then you MUST let the whisked eggs rest 5-7 minutes in order for the baking powder to begin to take effect. Then the butter must be hot enough (sizzling) to finish activating the baking powder. I realize Kit's instructions are very clear on this, but I have made these so many times that I don't look at the recipe anymore, and if I forget even one of these important steps, I just get ordinary, dry, crumbly eggs. Also, I find that adding the cheese before the eggs are cooked leaves them runny, so I like to cook the eggs until they are about 30 seconds from done, then fold in the cheese and remove from heat.
